findings.title: Action and inward self-formation
findings.claim: The focus's repeated good-action verb and its bad-action and face-harm contrast can carry a self-forming moral return: conduct is directed toward the agent's own inward state as well as toward its later consequence.
findings.mechanism: The two aḥsantum stems point good action toward anfusikum; 13:11 explicitly links a people's change to what is within themselves, while 45:15 states that good and bad deeds return for or against their doer. The focus's repeated سوء root then meets 40:45, where evil punishment closes around its planners. These contacts let the self-directed clause include inward formation and consequential return.
findings.reader_payoff: The return becomes perceptible within the acting self as well as in what later reaches the agent; the paired good and bad clauses retain their personal direction.
findings.containment: The inward-state resonance adds to the ordinary benefit or harm directed to oneself and does not replace it. The wider verses do not establish that their actors or events are identical to those in 17:7. The life-giving-soul branch is not activated here.

epistemic.reason: The focus carriers and wider Arabic surfaces are supplied, but target morphology is absent and the self-forming relation is an inference. The 17:15 and 17:19 echoes are retained only as an attributed legacy support.

findings.title: Dominion dismantled into matter
findings.claim: The focus's destruction can be read as material dismantling of an elevated order: the target can carry an upper-structure image by analogy, and the destructive verb can reach the made and raised works in pieces.
findings.mechanism: The doubled t-b-r verb and verbal noun carry destruction and physical breaking. 28:4 gives a wider instance of self-exaltation and social oppression; 7:137 says what Pharaoh's people made and raised was destroyed; the contact between the focus's raised target and those works activates B008 as an upper-structure analogy. 21:58 supplies an exact fragment image. The legacy support's 17:49-51 comparison adds a later question of restoration from matter. These relations move the close from abstract defeat toward the undoing of constructed power.
findings.reader_payoff: The final destruction can be seen as dismantling a dominated order in material terms, while the later restoration question keeps matter present as a possible beginning again.
findings.containment: The focus does not identify its target with Pharaoh's literal works or the idols in 21:58. B008 is an analogy, not a claim that the finite focus verb lexically means an added upper part. The 17:49-51 material comparison is legacy_unbound, and the packet does not specify the material composition of the focus's target.

epistemic.reason: The focus stems and exact Arabic in 28:4, 7:137, and 21:58 are supplied. The political and material synthesis is interpretive, and the additional 17:49-51 comparison comes only through a legacy reader support.

findings.title: Appointment and later gathering
findings.claim: The focus's promise of the latter can remain the promised historical event while carrying a wider horizon of fixed arrival, collective gathering, and possible afterlife resonance.
findings.mechanism: The carrier is waʿdu al-ākhirah within the focus's when-it-comes clause. 7:34 says a community's appointed term cannot be delayed or advanced; 17:103 describes Pharaoh's attempted expulsion reversing into drowning, and 17:104 repeats the latter-promise phrase before bringing the addressed people together. The restoration question in 17:51 and the first-creation and presentation scene in 18:48 let al-ākhirah also resonate with the afterlife. The contact adds an appointed and eschatological horizon to the historical event without merging them.
findings.reader_payoff: The focus's later promise holds a concrete historical return and a wider question of when people are gathered and restored.
findings.containment: No exact date is supplied, 7:34 does not identify its term with this promise, and 17:51 or 18:48 do not prove that the historical incursion is the afterlife event. The second-incursion reading remains intact.

epistemic.reason: The focus and cited target Arabic are supplied, but target morphology is absent and the temporal and afterlife links are contextual inferences from connection nominations.
